All-Di Copycat Breakfast Pizza Recipe 
If I were to make this again I would possibly use canned biscuits for the crust and roll them out as one big crust. The Aldi Sausage didn’t have much flavor so would swapped that out too. I think a premade Saysage gravy packet would be faster. All in all very good. It will have to do until they those pizzas make a return. 


Aldi Copy Cat Breakfast Pizza  (Half Sausage/Bacon, Pepper and Onion)


Crust: 
1 aldi pizza dough 


1 tb of butter


Toppings: 


2 slices of parcooked diced extra thick bacon

 
2 tablespoons sweet onion chopped 


2 tablespoons green peppers  chopped 


7 breakfast sausage links 


Cheese Mix: 


4 oz mild cheddar 


4 oz mozarella cheese 


2 oz rustic cheddar 


White Gravy: 


1 tablespoon sausage drippings


1 tablespoon oil 


2 tablespoons flour 


1 1/4 cup whole milk 


1/8 crushed red pepper flakes 


Poultry seasoning, sage and salt/pepper to taste 



1. Spread dough out on a 13 x 9 cookie sheet lined with parchment paper.


2. Add 1 tablespoon of melted butter over the dough

 
3. Let rise while you prepare everything else.


4. Take the breakfast sausages out of the casing and chopped into small pieces.


5. Sauté in a pan with 1 tablespoon of oil.


6. After the sausages have cooked removed from the pan and add 2 tablespoons of flour.


7. Cook the flour a few minutes, then add the milk and all of the other seasonings to taste. 


8. Par cook the diced bacon. I cooked mine in the air fryer for about eight minutes at 400°.


Assembley: 


1. Add half of the gravy to the pizza crust spread out evenly. You will have leftover gravy that you can freeze or serve with the pizza.


2. Sprinkle on most of the cheese and  reserve some for adding after you put on the toppings. 


3. Add the toppings and sprinkle on the remaining cheese 


3.  Bake at 450 for 8 to 15 minutes. You can also broil it for 2 minutes if you want a crispier cheese topping. 


Note: You will  have leftover gravy and sausages. You can save those for another meal. I didnt feel like Aldi sausages had alot of flavor so I would use a different kind next time.

I can’t get my veggie harvests to store more than a day or two. Looking for advice
This year has been great in the garden. I’m growing more than we can eat. My problem is storage. Everything seems to go bad so fast compared to store bought stuff. For example: I harvested some lettuce and stored it how I would store lettuce from the grocer. My lettuce wilted and was soggy the next day, meanwhile the store bought was still good a week later. I harvested my carrot crops and had to freeze them because they got soft after just 1 day. 

My blueberries, cherries, and strawberries go bad in the fridge within 2 days. While store bought are good for over a week. Any fruits, leafy veggies, root veggies, almost anything goes bad so fast. 

The only things I’ve successfully stored for more than a day or two are potatoes, garlic, onions, tomatoes, and peppers. 

I’ve tried storing on the counter, in the pantry, all separated, in the fridge, washed, unwashed, etc. I feel like no matter how I store things, nothing lasts as long as their store bought counterparts. How can I make things last without freezing? Book recommendations?

Give feedback on my wierd favorite.
First real post on reddit.

​

Anyway, I was looking for some feedback on a garnish/sauce that I regularly make that gets requested a LOT in my immediate family/circle of friends. But it is a bit of a wierd combination.. So I was mainly looking for feedback. How insane is this? Is it pretty standard, am I nuts for trying it? Both feedback, tips for improvement and general roasting is welcome.

​

The dish itself:

An onion/cola based sauce/garnish.

I roughly chop onions, lengthwise to preserve sweetness. A good 10 onions in the same general way one would prepare for onion soup.

In two big pans I slowly carmelise these, bringing them together into 1 saucepan once everything has reduced enough. (Deglazing the initial pans with some red wine vinegar to make sure no good flavors are thrown out, and to add some acidity.)

When I have my reduced onions simmering in the saucepan I add about 2 tablespoons of brown sugar. This leads to end result 1: Carmelized onion jam.

This used to be something I would make untill I started to experiment. The madness starts here.

Add 4 dried chili peppers and about 4 cloves of chopped garlic. Keep stirring.

Over time add about 1 1.5 litre bottle of cola. The basic sugared version. I would not know what the diet sugar substitutes do when heated.

When everything reduces down again, pick out the chili peppers. The heat and coke will have ensured that enough heat has seeped into the mixture.

​

The end result: A sauce/garnish that tastes at first sweet, cola,  then the hit of onion, and finally a very sharp chili aftertaste.

The fans here eat it cold as a garnish/side dish, or heated up as a sauce/condiment on burgers or other meat. A particular favorite is the whole burger deal with grilled buns, lettuce, tomato, burger, cheddar cheese, pickles and this garnish as the sauce.

​

I am looking forward to your insights!

​

Looking for feedback on Four Course Meal for friends
I have just a tiny bit of experience of teenage catering and a fair amount of home growth on technique and recipes and flavors. I wanted to serve my friends (and my Polish parents) a four course Polish meal. I've read Michal Korkosz's Fresh From Poland, and I've gotten familiar with the slightly eastern parts of Polish seasoning. So I wanted to lay out the courses for feedback and advice (or solicit a more appropriate subreddit for this).

* First drink: silverberry nalewka (aged vodka fruit infusion) or blackcurrant italian soda
* Amuse bouche: fresh rye sourdough rolls torn open smeared with pate, light sprinkle of scallions and shredded cucumber. Pate is mushroom/walnut or a duck/pork blend, both marjoram and pepper forward. Drink pairing: beaujolais/burgundy (need a suggestion for non-alcohol drink pairing)
* Salad: Apple leek shaved beet radicchio with vegan creamy poppyseed dressing, rye croutons. Drink pairing: tatanka, a mixed drink of bison grass vodka and cider (seltzer for mocktail)
* Main: Bigos, hunters stew with red wine, fermented (and non-) cabbage, and dried (and roasted mushroom, mustard coriander caraway. Then venison/bison/smoked pork or mushroom/beans. Rye sourdough rolls return. Drink pairing: orange wine or wildberry ice tea
* Dessert: Vegan brownies with oatmilk chocolate ice cream (or sanguinaccio dolce, pig’s blood custard). Drink pairing: coffee liqueur with vodka and creme de cacao or black tea
* (Available between courses): lemon ginger sorbet

A fair amount I’ll be able to make in advance, and I’m paying a catering acquaintance to do the plating, bussing, and monitoring bakes/thaws. Guests will serve their own wine.

Thoughts on flavor profile, progression, logistics? Thanks for the feedback

Saturday Breakfast Salad - Serves 1 

Handful of greens like kale, arugula, romaine spinach, whatever is on hand

2-3 sausage links,  or 1/4 sausage crumbles or left over steak, or bacon precooked or not

Egg

Left over bread

Seasonings to taste I use Penzey's seasoned salt 

Scant 1/2 to 1 Tbsp of lemon juice 

Olive oil.

Preheat broiler or use your toaster. I don't own a toaster so broiler it is. Lightly bylrush bread with a little olive oil if broiling, do this step after toasting if your toasting. Broil your bread until browned. Cut into cubes set aside.

In small bowl put greens sprinkle a little seasoning on it and a little olive toss gently to coat Add a little lemon juice and toss set aside.

If you need to cook your breakfast meat or reheat it do it now. Cut into bite size pieces or crumble and put on top of salad. Add your croutons. 

 gFry egg to your yolk doness preference. I like mine over easy. The yolk will act as an emulsifier but if you don't like runny egg yolk then the olive oil on the leaves is a fine sub. If sunny side up or over easy put ont op of greens and croutons gently, otherwise just put scrambled on top. Lightly season with whatever your using and add a little more lemon juice on top.

If your yolk is runny as you cut into it it will coat the croutons and greens creating a really nice tangy dressing effect. 

Enjoy!

Tahitian 'Ota 'ika - Lime Cooked Fish with Coconut Milk and Veggies (kosher and low calorie)
Yesterday there was a post about someone looking for beet recipes because they're in season and their father was wanting them to cook something with them. It reminded me of one of my absolute favorite dishes, it's from a blogger so I'll post a link to it in the stickied "Youtube/Content Roundup-Thread" in case anyone is interested in giving it a look.

It's an Oceanian dish, similar to Ceviche or Hawaiian Poke, with variants from Tonga, Tahiti, Samoa, Papa New Guinea, and New Zealand. It's also similar to other recipes throughout the world. There's a Wiki page with more information if it interests you to explore other dishes similar to it!

*Course:* **Main** | *Servings:* **4** | *Cuisine:* **French** |
*Prep Time:* **30 Minutes** | *Cook Time:* **1 Hour** | *Total Time:* **1 Hour 30 Minutes**
 
# Ingredients

* 1 lb fresh, sushi-grade fish; ahi tuna, yellowfin tuna, halibut or snapper

* 4 cups cold water

* 2 tbsp salt *plus more for seasoning*

* 3/4 cup freshly squeezed lime juice

* 3/4-1 cup whole fat coconut milk *fresh is best*

* pepper to taste

# Optional Ingredients

* 1 whole carrot *peeled and grated*

* 6 oz cucumber *seeded and diced*

* 1/3 cup scallions *sliced into rings*

* 1 whole tomato *seeded and diced, squeezed in cheesecloth to remove excess liquid*

* unsweetened fresh coconut shreds

# Instructions

    1. Dice the fish into 3/4 inch pieces, then cover with cold water and 2 tbsp salt 
    (add a few ice cubes if the water is not chilled). Let the fish sit for 20 minutes.
    Meanwhile, squeeze your limes to juice them.

    2. Drain the fish and pat it dry. Submerge the fish in fresh lime juice; you will 
    need between 3/4 cup and 1 cup to cover. Let the fish marinate, stirring 
    occasionally, for 15-30 minutes until the edges are opaque and the center 
    of each piece is still pink.

    3. While fish is marinating, prepare your vegetables. You may use any or all 
    of the vegetables listed above; reserve a little of each on the side for garnish.

    4. Drain the lime juice from the fish, then return the fish to the bowl. Stir in 
    the fresh vegetables and coconut milk. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
    Allow the mixture to marinate in the refrigerator for 15-30 minutes.

    5. Serve cold garnished with fresh vegetables. May be enjoyed over coconut 
    rice for a more filling entrée.

# Nutrition

*Calories:* **282kcal** | *Carbohydrates:* **5g** |*Protein:* **28g**
*Saturated Fat:* **10g** | *Cholesterol:* **43mg** | *Sodium:* ** 3556mg** 
*Potassium:* **592mg** | *Fiber:* **2g** | *Sugar:* **3g** 
*Vitamin A:* **3010IU** | *Vitamin C:* **10.4mg** | *Calcium:* **40mg** 
*Iron:* **2.2mg**

Want to make smash burgers for a Uni event, would love advice.

There’s an upcoming event in my university and they bring food trucks / stands and what not to serve students something to eat. My friends give compliments to my smash burgers whenever they’re over (they can go overboard with the glazing though that’s why I’m here) so I thought maybe it would be a good idea to participate and make new friends on the way.


I make my smash burgers at home in a stainless steel pan on a *gas stovetop*. I have no experience making smash burgers any other way.

I learnt that a griddle (the big one) is the best option for a smash burgers but I don’t think it’s the smartest investment considering 1) I don’t have space nor will I use it at home 2) I’m only planning on doing this for fun in the upcoming event 3) I won’t have access to gas in the event. Therefore whatever I’m cooking on has to be ELECTRIC. Favorite ways to reuse recyclables/trash for gardening?
Here are a few of my favorite uses:

1. Cut the top off of half gallon milk cartons (cardboard) and use for DEEP transplant pots for tomato seedlings once they outgrow their starter cells.   Be sure to punch drainage holes in bottom.  
2. Cut bottom/base off of food-safe plastic gallon jugs (distilled water, milk) and use as mini cloches for cold weather.  Save the top and you have adjustable ventilation! Lettuce grows so much faster under these in early spring, and it better protected from some pests.  Take the lid off if it's hot; replace the lid at night. The translucence can also help with shielding from sun scald during hardening off or early transplant days.  They can be stacked for temporary storage, looped on a fence post, or tied together by the handles and then (eventually) recycled.
3. Save the bottom of the gallon jug for covering shorter seedlings from frost/cold or and/or use as a small tray/work surface for various gardening tasks.
4. Deep plastic lids (peanut butter jars, mayo) make good saucers for under small pots, such as solo cups with seedling starts.  
5. Save mesh produce bags to use as "slings" to help support heavy squash or fruits on a trellis. 
6. Save plastic bread and roll bags for storing tall greens with stems attached (chard, etc).  

Hope these tips might be useful to somebody else. Any other ideas?

The store bought pickle bloodlines are weak and could never survive the winter - instead here is my homemade pickle recipe!
I love pickles but most store bought pickles are often expensive and don't even taste that good. It's really easy to make you own pickles cheaply that taste powerful, spicy, and amazing. Here's my recipe for all you pickle aficionados out there.

**Vegetables**

* Persian cucumbers (or small Kirby snack cucumbers)
* Additions: Small tender carrots, asparagus, okra, green beans, beats, radish
   * *Wash well and cut the tips off the cucumbers*
   * *Add in a few other vegetables for color and variety*

**Brine**

* 5 Cups Vinegar (5% acetic acid)
* 4 Cups Water
* 6 Tbsp Sea Salt
* 9 Tbsp Sugar
* 2 Tsp Ca-Lactate
   * *Mix together and boil*
   * *Total is 9 cups (2.1 litres) of brine*

**Aromatics**

* Fresh Dill Leaves
* Garlic
* Bulb Onions
* Serrano Peppers
* Turmeric Root
   * *Add lots of these as they will be the dominant flavours given to the pickle*
   * *Usually best to cut in half or dice roots to steep in the brine*

**Spices**

* Black Pepper Corns
* Coriander Seeds
* Mustard Seeds
* Bay Leaves
* Korean Smoked Pepper flakes
   * *Add as whole seeds and leaves*
   * *If adding pepper flakes try and use larger less powdery ones*

**NOTES:**

* Use large jars to have space for the vegetables and the aromatics, or use smaller jars and cut the vegetables to size. Jars with vacuum pop-lids are ideal or using glass jars with a rubber seal. Clean and place them and their lids upside down in boiling water for 5 minutes to sterilize. Layer the vegetables and aromatics in them and pour the hot brine over top leaving a small air gap at the top to avoid anoxic brine that can be dangerous if not completely sterilized. Cover with lids of bowls and let cool till warm but able to be held in the hand then seal and put in the fridge. These are fridge pickles so only keep for a few months, if you're making shelf stable preserve pickles read up on sterilization. Shake the jars every day for the first 3 days to ensure the brine is mixed thoroughly as the vegetables equilibrate. Should be delicious after about a week, but may need longer for larger, denser vegetables.
* The brine ratio is 1.25 parts of 5% vinegar to 1 part water, slightly more powerful than the minimum 1:1 ratio and should pickle easily even if the jars are densely packed without being overpowering. Use sea or kosher salt as these are usually unadulterated and do not contain any added iodine or silicate anti-caking agents that can cloud the brine. Sugar helps to mellow the acidic taste of the brine but can also make them too sweet if too much is used. Calcium is added to keep the vegetables crisp and snappy. Calcium-Chloride can be used but is bitter tasting, aka HCl, so use Calcium-Lactate instead (easy to find foodgrade online). As a bonus the Calcium-Lactate forms lactic-acid which is the delicious sour taste of fermented pickles. CaCl is 36% Calcium and CaLactate is 18% Calcium so need twice as much in a recipe but as it tastes good you don't need to worry as much so use more for sliced vegetables that are more likely to lose crispness. Commonly 0.25-0.75 tsp of CaCl per litre is used so 0.5-1.5 tsp of Ca-Lactate per litre is enough for whole cucumbers but can also slow the pickling of whole vegetables as they stay denser so let them brine longer before eating.
* Persian cucumbers are usually the best and easiest to find vegetable for pickling though other vegetables are also good. Cut the tips off to keep from getting mushy and allow better brine penetration. The larger and denser the vegetable the less it will pickle so thinner tender vegetables are best or slice them into smaller pieces. The best places to find them are usually indian or middle eastern grocery and wholesale markets as they are well priced and sell in bulk. Lots of vegetables and spices to try pickling with can be found in them and usually large bundles of fresh dill leaves (and you want lots of fresh dill for your pickles). Aromatics and spices are all variable and to taste but add lots of flavor. It is best to add much more than you would for cooking as these are only flavouring the brine and won't be as powerful as they would be when cooked into a dish.
